title: What Was the War on Terror?
gist: Reviewing Peter Bergen's 'All the Presidents' Wars,' Philip Gordon argues the 25-year, roughly $4-6 trillion U.S. war on terror achieved its core goal (no major foreign-directed terrorist attack on U.S. soil since 9/11) but at wildly disproportionate human and financial cost driven by strategic overreach — trying to transform the Middle East by force rather than narrowly destroying al-Qaeda — and concludes that under the second Trump administration, the war-on-terror paradigm that defined U.S. foreign policy for a generation is now effectively over.

themes.theme: The war on terror's 25-year arc across four presidents

insights.claim: George W. Bush was elected in 2000 on a platform of a 'humble' foreign policy skeptical of nation-building, but by 2003 his administration had launched an invasion of Iraq aimed at transforming and democratizing the entire Middle East, and the resulting global war on terror became the primary paradigm for U.S. foreign policy, comparable to the Cold War's role from 1947 to 1989.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: Frames the war on terror as a multi-decade, Cold-War-scale strategic paradigm shift born from a reversal of Bush's original 'humble' foreign policy stance — useful context for assessing how quickly stated foreign-policy doctrines can invert under crisis pressure.
insights.quote: Singularly focused on the need to prevent another 9/11, Bush’s modest approach to world affairs morphed into the so-called global war on terror that became the primary paradigm for U.S. foreign policy, akin to the role of the Cold War from 1947 until 1989.

insights.claim: Barack Obama, despite skepticism of military intervention, ordered a surge of nearly 50,000 additional U.S. troops into Afghanistan between 2009 and 2012 (bringing the total to around 100,000) and turned drone warfare from a novel tactic into a routine tool of U.S. policy.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: Documents the scale of Obama's Afghanistan surge (to ~100,000 troops) and his institutionalization of drone warfare as standard policy — relevant precedent for assessing how quickly an incoming administration's stated restraint can give way to escalation.
insights.quote: Barack Obama, although skeptical of U.S. military intervention and elected in part because of his opposition to the Iraq war, found himself not just fighting but expanding the war in Afghanistan—where between 2009 and 2012 he ordered a surge of nearly 50,000 additional U.S. troops (bringing the total to around 100,000)—and turning lethal drone warfare from a novel tactic into a routine tool.

insights.claim: Every U.S. president since Bill Clinton has come to office vowing to reduce American involvement in the Middle East, and every one has instead found himself dragged back into the same policies and the same wars — until Biden's 2021 Afghanistan withdrawal broke that pattern, at great cost.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: Establishes a multi-decade base rate — every president since Clinton has been pulled back into Middle East military commitments despite stated intentions to reduce involvement — a useful prior when assessing the credibility of the current Trump administration's claims to be ending the war on terror.
insights.quote: Every president since Bill Clinton came to office vowing to reduce American involvement in the Middle East, and every president has found himself dragged back into the same policies and the same wars.

insights.claim: Biden's chaotic 2021 Afghanistan withdrawal — implementing a deal inherited from Trump — left 13 U.S. service members and hundreds of Afghans dead, stranded thousands of Afghan allies, and inflicted lasting damage to Biden's public standing, 'a blow from which he never recovered.'
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: Documents the specific human and political cost of the 2021 Afghanistan withdrawal, a landmark event whose reputational damage to Biden is cited as durable and largely unrecovered — relevant to assessing political risk of similarly abrupt military disengagements.
insights.quote: The chaotic U.S. withdrawal left 13 service members (and hundreds of Afghans) dead, stranded thousands of Afghans who had worked with the United States, and damaged the American public’s perception of Biden, a blow from which he never recovered.

themes.theme: The staggering costs versus the narrow achievement

insights.claim: According to Bergen's estimates, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan cost the United States at least $4 trillion (or $6 trillion including military pensions), killed roughly 7,000 U.S. service members and an estimated 8,000 contractors, and (by conservative estimates) killed 200,000 Iraqis and tens of thousands of Afghans.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: Provides the definitive cost accounting ($4-6 trillion, ~15,000 U.S. dead including contractors, 200,000+ Iraqi dead) for the two central wars of the war-on-terror era, a critical baseline for evaluating cost-effectiveness of any future large-scale military intervention.
insights.quote: According to Bergen’s estimates, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan cost the United States at least $4 trillion ($6 trillion, if military pensions are included). Some 7,000 U.S. service members lost their lives, alongside an estimated 8,000 contractors. Conservative estimates suggest that 200,000 Iraqis were killed, as were tens of thousands of Afghans.

insights.claim: The war on terror's primary goal — preventing another large-scale, lethal terrorist attack by foreign groups on U.S. soil for 25 years after 9/11 — has been achieved, even though few Americans in late 2001 would have predicted such a stretch without one.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: The core stated objective of the entire war-on-terror era was met, but at a cost (per the prior insight) wildly disproportionate to the threat, framing the war on terror as a case study in expensive strategic overreach relative to a narrower achievable goal.
insights.quote: In late 2001, few Americans would have predicted that the next 25 years would pass without any large-scale, lethal terrorist attack carried out by foreign groups on U.S. soil. That was the primary goal of the war on terror, and it has been achieved.

insights.claim: Al-Qaeda and ISIS are now shadows of their former selves, lacking charismatic leadership and territorial control, but remain capable of mass-casualty attacks, as demonstrated by 2024 ISIS-affiliate bombings in Moscow and Iran.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: Confirms that despite the war on terror's near-total dismantlement of jihadist territorial control, residual mass-casualty attack capability persists — worth watching for tail-risk terrorism events even amid declining Western policy attention.
insights.quote: Those groups and their offshoots are still capable of mass-casualty attacks, as bombings by an ISIS affiliate in Moscow and in Iran in 2024 demonstrated, but are now shadows of their former selves

themes.theme: Strategic overreach, not just tactical error

insights.claim: Gordon argues Bergen sometimes falls into the trap of framing the war on terror's failures as tactical miscalculations or flawed implementation, when the greater error was the fundamental strategic decision to declare an all-encompassing war on a tactic and attempt to transform an entire region by military force.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: A key analytical distinction for evaluating any future large-scale military campaign: whether critique should focus on execution or on the underlying strategic premise itself — a useful framework for post-mortems on interventionist foreign policy.
insights.quote: Bergen sometimes falls into the familiar trap of suggesting the main problems with the war on terror were tactical miscalculations or flawed implementation rather than the fundamental strategic error of declaring an all-encompassing war on a tactic and trying to transform an entire region with military force.

insights.claim: Paul Bremer's May 2003 decisions to dissolve the entire Iraqi army and fire tens of thousands of Baath Party officials helped create a well-armed, resentful insurgent force that U.S. troops would fight in Iraqi cities for years, and no one in the Bush administration ever took responsibility for those missteps.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: Names the specific administrative decision (Iraqi army dissolution) most directly responsible for spawning the insurgency, a textbook case of how post-conflict administrative choices can generate the very threat a military intervention was meant to eliminate.
insights.quote: Chief among those were the decisions made in May 2003 by Paul Bremer, often referred to as Washington’s “viceroy” in Baghdad, to dissolve the entire Iraqi army and fire tens of thousands of Baath Party officials, thus helping to create a well-armed, resentful insurgent force

insights.claim: Gordon argues that had Bush focused narrowly on destroying al-Qaeda and capturing bin Laden rather than pursuing the Taliban and invading Iraq, the U.S. might have ended the global terrorist threat before being dragged into a costly 25-year conflict.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: Articulates the counterfactual 'narrow counterterrorism' alternative strategy explicitly, a benchmark against which the actual expansive war on terror's costs can be judged.
insights.quote: Had Bush focused on al-Qaeda and bin Laden, rather than the Taliban and Iraq, he might have been able to destroy that group and its leaders and the global terrorist threat before getting dragged into a costly 25-year conflict.
insights.locator: section on alternatives to the war on terror

themes.theme: The war on terror's end under the second Trump administration

insights.claim: Under the second Trump administration, the war on terror appears to be ending: Trump has framed interventions in the Caribbean and Venezuela as fights against 'narcoterrorists' and his February 2026 attack on Iran as a strike against 'the world's number one state sponsor of terror,' but combating legacy groups like al-Qaeda and ISIS now ranks far below his other strategic priorities and receives fewer resources and attention than at any point in the past 25 years.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: Signals a genuine paradigm shift in U.S. foreign policy priorities away from counterterrorism toward narco-trafficking and state-adversary framing — relevant for assessing where future U.S. military attention and defense spending will concentrate.
insights.quote: Trump has framed his interventions in the Caribbean and Venezuela as campaigns against “narcoterrorists” and justified his February 2026 attack on Iran as a strike against “the world’s number one state sponsor of terror.” But in practice, combating what the administration calls “legacy” groups such as al-Qaeda and ISIS ranks far below Trump’s other strategic priorities
insights.locator: section on the current Trump administration

insights.claim: Trump's November 2025 National Security Strategy barely mentions global jihadism and instead emphasizes shedding 'forever global burdens,' signaling an explicit deprioritization of the counterterrorism paradigm that dominated U.S. foreign policy for a quarter century.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated policy document (Nov 2025 NSS) marking the formal deprioritization of counterterrorism in official U.S. strategy — a useful reference point for tracking the shift in defense budget and force-posture priorities.
insights.quote: Far from prioritizing the fight against global jihadism, Trump’s November 2025 National Security Strategy barely mentions it and instead emphasizes shedding “forever global burdens.”
insights.locator: section on the current Trump administration

themes.theme: New historical revelations from Bergen's reporting

insights.claim: Bergen argues persuasively that Osama bin Laden was almost certainly in the Tora Bora cave complex in eastern Afghanistan in late 2001, and that a failure to commit sufficient U.S. forces there — partly because military and political attention was already shifting toward Iraq — allowed him to escape into Pakistan.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: Directly links the pivot toward Iraq to bin Laden's escape at Tora Bora — a concrete causal claim tying resource misallocation to the war on terror's most consequential unresolved failure (a decade-long manhunt).
insights.quote: He convincingly argues that despite Bush officials’ claims of uncertainty, bin Laden was almost definitely in the Tora Bora cave complex in eastern Afghanistan in late 2001, and the failure to commit sufficient U.S. forces—in part because military and political attention was already shifting toward Iraq—allowed him to escape into Pakistan.

insights.claim: Contrary to common assumptions that bin Laden wanted the 9/11 attacks to draw the U.S. into a prolonged Middle East war, he actually believed the strikes would push the U.S. to withdraw its forces from the region — modeled on how the 1983 Beirut Marine barracks bombing and the 1993 'Black Hawk Down' incident in Mogadishu had spurred U.S. withdrawals from Lebanon and Somalia.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: A striking historical reframing: bin Laden's strategic calculus was essentially the opposite of what happened, showing that even terrorist leaders can badly miscalculate the consequences of their attacks — a nuance relevant to threat-modeling of future asymmetric actors.
insights.quote: contrary to common suggestions that bin Laden believed the 9/11 attacks would draw the United States into a bloody Middle East war, he in fact believed the opposite: that the strikes on American soil would encourage the United States to withdraw its forces from the region

insights.claim: Gordon concludes the primary lesson of the war on terror is that legitimate fears combined with a quest for absolute security can lead a great power to overreach, with consequences that no one can predict or easily reverse.
insights.speaker: Philip H. Gordon
insights.so_what: A durable strategic-risk framework applicable well beyond counterterrorism: any policy driven by an 'absolute security' mandate (whether against terrorism, pandemics, or AI risk) carries a structural overreach risk worth pricing into long-term forecasts.
insights.quote: Every citizen—and especially those who will make U.S. policy in the future—should reckon with the primary lesson of All the Presidents’ Wars: that legitimate fears and a quest for absolute security can lead a great power to overreach, with consequences no one can predict or easily reverse.
